derivations.claim: The two parenthesizations of a triple product in $G_d$ have the same central coordinate, since both give $\theta+\theta'+\theta''-v'\cdot a-v''\cdot a-v''\cdot a'$. The identity is $(0,0,0)$ and the inverse of $(a,v,\theta)$ is $(-a,-v,-\theta-v\cdot a)$. Multiplying by $(0,0,\eta)$ on either side adds $\eta$ to the central coordinate and leaves $(a,v)$ fixed, so $Z$ is central; the quotient forgets $\theta$ and is the additive group $\mathbb R^{2d}$.
By [A2] and [F1], $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the stated pairing is a complex Hilbert space, so the operator definitions act on the required Hilbert space.

Translation is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes by [F2], and $\|T(a)f\|_2^2=\int |f(x-a)|^2dx=\int |f(x)|^2dx$ by [F3]. The map is linear with inverse $T(-a)$; hence it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.
The multiplier $e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}$ is measurable and has modulus one by [F4], so $B_m(v)$ preserves the norm. It is linear with inverse $B_m(-v)$; hence it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.

For almost every $x$, $(B_m(v)T(a)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}f(x-a)$ while $(T(a)B_m(v)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot(x-a)/\hbar}f(x-a)$. Their ratio is the constant $e^{imv\cdot a/\hbar}$, proving the commutation identity. Multiplying it on the right by $B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$ gives the displayed loop identity.

Let $g=u+iw\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$. For the unitary families established in steps 2.1 and 2.2, [F10] gives $u,w\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$; applying [F9] to each component and using $\|h+ik\|_2^2=\|h\|_2^2+\|k\|_2^2$ yields $\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2\to0$ as $a\to a_0$. If $v_n\to v_0$, then $|e^{im(v_n-v_0)\cdot x/\hbar}-1|^2|g(x)|^2\to0$ pointwise and is bounded by $4|g(x)|^2$, which is integrable. Dominated convergence [F12] gives $\|B_m(v_n)g-B_m(v_0)g\|_2\to0$. Since Euclidean parameter spaces are metric, both orbit maps are continuous on this dense smooth subspace.

For arbitrary $f\in\mathcal H$, approximate it in $L^2$ by $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ using [F8]. Unitarity in steps 2.1 and 2.2 gives $\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2\le2\|f-g\|_2+\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2$, and the analogous estimate for $B_m(v)$; letting the approximation error be arbitrarily small extends both continuities to every $f$. Moreover,
$$\|\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)f-\Pi_m(a_0,v_0,\theta_0)f\|_2\le |e^{im\theta/\hbar}-e^{im\theta_0/\hbar}|\|f\|_2+\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2+\|(B_m(v)-B_m(v_0))T(a_0)f\|_2,$$
so the orbit map of $\Pi_m$ is norm-continuous on the product Euclidean group.

Using $T(a)B_m(v')=e^{-imv'\cdot a/\hbar}B_m(v')T(a)$ from step 3.1 and the addition laws of the two families, multiplication gives $\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)\Pi_m(a',v',\theta')=\Pi_m(a+a',v+v',\theta+\theta'-v'\cdot a)$. By step 1.1 this is the group law; the operators are unitary by steps 2.1 and 2.2, and their orbit maps are continuous by step 4.1. Thus $\Pi_m$ is a unitary representation by [F5], and $\Pi_m(0,0,\eta)=e^{im\eta/\hbar}I$ is its central character.

For a finite direct sum the central subgroup acts as $\bigoplus_j e^{im_j\eta/\hbar}I_j$. If $m_j\ne m_k$, choose $0<|\eta|<2\pi\hbar/|m_j-m_k|$; then $e^{im_j\eta/\hbar}\ne e^{im_k\eta/\hbar}$. Hence the central characters are pairwise distinct.

Substituting $p=mv$ into the displayed Weyl formula gives $W(a,mv)=e^{-imv\cdot a/(2\hbar)}B_m(v)T(a)$. Direct multiplication gives $W(a,p)W(a',p')=e^{-i\omega((a,p),(a',p'))/(2\hbar)}W(a+a',p+p')$. The published model result [F7] verifies this system is irreducible and regular, and [F6] gives unitary equivalence for every other system with the same finite phase space and nonzero parameter $1/\hbar$.

derivations.claim: Each $\sigma_i$ is self-adjoint, satisfies $\sigma_i^2=I$, and has eigenvalues $1,-1$, so $A_i(t)=e^{-it\sigma_i/2}$ is unitary with determinant $1$ and obeys $A_i(t+u)=A_i(t)A_i(u)$; in particular $A_z(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-it/2},e^{it/2})$. For $U(t):=D(A_z(t))$, the generator convention gives $U'(0)=-iJ_z$. Since this one-parameter subgroup is abelian, $U(t+h)=U(t)U(h)=U(h)U(t)$; differentiating the two products at $h=0$ gives $U'(t)=U(t)(-iJ_z)=(-iJ_z)U(t)$. Differentiating $e^{itJ_z}U(t)$ now shows it is constant, hence $D(A_z(t))=e^{-itJ_z}$.

By [F1], choose the orthonormal spin-$s$ basis with $J_zv_k=(s-k)v_k$ for $k=0,\ldots,2s$. The matrix exponential power series acts on each eigenvector by its scalar exponential, so $e^{-i2\pi J_z}v_k=e^{-i2\pi(s-k)}v_k=(-1)^{2s}v_k$, since $e^{i2\pi k}=1$.
$A_z(2\pi)=-I$, so step 1.1 gives $D(-I)=e^{-i2\pi J_z}$. Step 1.2 evaluates this operator on an orthonormal basis and proves $D(-I)=(-1)^{2s}I_V$.

By [F2], every $R\in SO(3)$ has exactly two lifts $W$ and $-W$. The representation law gives $D(-W)=D(-I)D(W)=(-1)^{2s}D(W)$ by step 2.1. The scalar is a phase, so the projective class $[D(W)]\in PU(V)$ is independent of the lift. If $R_1=\rho(W_1)$ and $R_2=\rho(W_2)$, then $W_1W_2$ lifts $R_1R_2$, and $[D(W_1W_2)]=[D(W_1)][D(W_2)]$; hence the ray map is a homomorphism. It is continuous because the covering has local inverse sections and $D$ is continuous.

If $s$ is integer, $(-1)^{2s}=1$, so $D(W)$ is independent of the lift; defining $\widetilde D(R)=D(W)$ gives a unitary representation because products of lifts lift the product, as in step 3.1, and it is continuous by the same local-section argument. If $s$ is half-integer, $(-1)^{2s}=-1$, so the two lifts $I$ and $-I$ of the identity have images $I_V$ and $-I_V$; these differ since $V\ne\{0\}$. Therefore $D$ cannot factor as a unitary representation through $\rho$, although its projective class from step 3.1 does factor.

derivations.claim: Since $I=\sum_iP_i$ and $A=\sum_jP_jAP_j$, expansion gives $\rho A=\sum_{i,j}P_i\rho P_jAP_j$. This is a finite sum, and every summand is trace class by [F1], so taking its trace term by term is legitimate.

If $i\ne j$, cyclicity in [F1] gives $\operatorname{tr}(P_i\rho P_jAP_j)=\operatorname{tr}(P_jP_i\rho P_jA)=0$, since orthogonality gives $P_jP_i=0$. The remaining terms are $\operatorname{tr}(P_i\rho P_iAP_i)$. Because $A$ is block diagonal, $P_i\rho P_iA=P_i\rho P_iAP_i$, so their sum is exactly $\operatorname{tr}((\sum_iP_i\rho P_i)A)$. This proves the statement.

derivations.claim: Put $\theta=mv\cdot a/\hbar$. The loop identity in [F1] gives the scalar operator $e^{i\theta}I$ on the system Hilbert space, so one isolated branch acquires only a global phase.

On the path-system space $\mathbb C^2\otimes L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ define the controlled loop $C=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes L+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes I$, where $L=B_m(v)T(a)B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$. By step 1.1, $C=U_\theta\otimes I$ with $U_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},1)$. Equip the path space with inner product $u^*w$ and put $u_+=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2$. The recombining path overlap is the matrix coefficient $u_+^*U_\theta u_+=(1+e^{i\theta})/2$, whose squared modulus is $(2+2\cos\theta)/4=\cos^2(\theta/2)$ by the cosine double-angle identity. If the same scalar is applied to both arms, the path gate is $e^{i\theta}I_2$, whose matrix coefficient has squared modulus $1$.

Interchanging the finite indices $j,k$ in the second sum and commuting complex scalars makes the sums equal, so $\operatorname{tr}(QP-PQ)=0$.
Taking the trace in [A1] gives $0=i\hbar\operatorname{tr}(I_d)=i\hbar d$, which is impossible because $d\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$. Therefore the proposed universal existence statement is false.
